bio.en: Wes Kao co-created the Alt-MBA with Seth Godin and co-founded Maven, and is a writer and educator focused on operations, management, and executive communication.
bio.zh: Wes Kao 与 Seth Godin 共同创造了 Alt-MBA，并联合创立了 Maven，她是一位专注于运营、管理与高管沟通的写作者和教育者。

summary.en: Wes shares how to communicate as an executive and increase your influence, built around the idea that the biggest problem in communication is the illusion that it has taken place. She covers being specific instead of vague, earning trust through clarity, and why strong communication compounds across a career. The episode is a practical guide to a high-leverage skill most people underinvest in.
summary.zh: Wes 分享了如何以高管的方式沟通、提升影响力，其核心是：沟通中最大的问题，就是“以为沟通已经发生”的错觉。她涵盖了用具体取代含糊、通过清晰赢得信任，以及为什么出色的沟通会在整个职业生涯中产生复利。本期是关于一项大多数人投入不足的高杠杆技能的务实指南。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I think that most people assume that their boss has to manage them and they feel a little bit resentful that, why should I manage my boss? They're getting paid more. They are my manager. They have more responsibility.
turns.zh: 我认为大多数人都会认为他们的老板应该管理他们，而当被问到“为什么我要管理我的老板？”时，他们会感到有些不满。毕竟老板的薪资更高，他们才是我的上级，承担着更多的责任。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And you can continue to think that way and your career might be fine, but if you embrace that if you manage your boss, they're going to appreciate you much more, you're going to get more opportunities, you're going to have more trust with them, there's all these great things that happen when you decide to manage up.
turns.zh: 你可以继续这样想，或许你的职业生涯也能顺风顺水，但如果你选择主动管理你的老板，他们会对你更加赞赏，为你创造更多机会，与你建立更深的信任——当你决定向上管理时，总会收获诸多好处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wes Kao is the co-founder of Maven, a cohort-based learning platform that I used to create my own course on product management. But even more interestingly, she's helped folks like Seth Godin start his altMBA course, which is legendary. She's also helped people like David Perell, Tiago Forte, Scott Galloway, and even Morning Brew build their cohort-based courses. She's one of the smartest people I have ever met on the art of teaching and I've learned a ton from her.
turns.zh: 韦斯·考（Wes Kao）是Maven的联合创始人，我曾在该平台上创建自己的产品管理课程。更令人惊叹的是，她帮助赛斯·高丁（Seth Godin）创办了传奇的altMBA课程，还助力大卫·佩雷尔（David Perell）、蒂亚戈·福特（Tiago Forte）、斯科特·加洛韦（Scott Galloway）等行业领袖开发基于同期学习的课程。她是我见过最精通教学艺术的人之一，从她身上我学到了太多宝贵经验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in our chat, we cover a concept I love called the super specific who. We talk about the state change method and how using this idea, you'll run better meetings. We look at a bunch of advice for why you should spend time managing up and how to manage up effectively. We talk about a bunch of ways to write better, tips for saying no, and a bunch of other really interesting topics. I always have such a good time chatting with Wes, and I hope that you learn as much from this chat as I did. And with that, I bring you Wes Kao.
turns.zh: 在我们的对话中，我们探讨了一个我深爱的概念——超级具体的"who"。我们讨论了状态转换方法，以及如何运用这一理念提升会议效率。我们还分享了为何要投入时间向上管理以及如何有效做到这一点的建议。我们还探讨了多项写作技巧、拒绝他人的诀窍等诸多有趣话题。与韦斯的对话总是充满乐趣，希望你能像我一样从中收获满满。现在，让我们迎来韦斯·考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Modern Treasury. Modern Treasury is a next generation operating system for moving and tracking money. They're modernizing the developer tools and financial processes for companies managing complex payment flows. Think digital wallets, fiat crypto on-ramps, ride sharing marketplaces, instant lending and more. They work with high growth companies like Gusto, Hype, ClassPass and Marqeta.
turns.zh: 本期节目由Modern Treasury赞助。Modern Treasury是一款用于资金流转与追踪的下一代操作系统。他们正在为管理复杂支付流程的企业，现代化开发者工具与财务流程。涵盖数字钱包、法币加密货币入口、网约车平台、即时借贷等场景。他们与Gusto、Hype、ClassPass、Marqeta等高增长公司合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Modern Treasury's robust APIs allow engineering to build payment flows right into your product while finance can monitor and approve everything through a sleek and modern web dashboard, enabling realtime payments, automatic reconciliation, continuous accounting and compliance solutions. Modern Treasury's platform is used to reconcile over $3 billion per month.
turns.zh: Modern Treasury强大的API接口支持工程团队将支付流程直接嵌入产品，而财务团队可通过时尚现代的Web仪表板监控并审批所有操作，实现实时支付、自动对账、持续记账与合规解决方案。Modern Treasury平台每月处理超30亿美元的资金对账。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're one of the hottest young FinTech startups on the market today, having raised funding from top firms like Benchmark, Altimeter, SVB Capital, Salesforce Ventures, and Y Combinator. Check them out at moderntreasury.com.
turns.zh: 作为当下市场上最热门的年轻金融科技初创公司之一，他们已成功从Benchmark、Altimeter、SVB Capital、Salesforce Ventures和Y Combinator等顶级风投机构获得融资。欢迎访问moderntreasury.com了解更多信息。

With Berbix, businesses can quickly and easily verify someone's identity through their government issued ID and real-time selfie.

With Berbix, you can grow revenue by instantly verifying a customer's drivers license, passport, or ID card. turns.zh: 无需编码、低代码或完全集成，仅需一个下午即可快速上手Berbix。访问berbix.com/start即可立即开始。网址是B-E-R-B-I-X.com/start。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wes, I have learned so much from you over the years in so many different ways, while building my course, through your writing, through your tweets. And generally you're just a super fascinating human that I love this excuse to get to learn more about you and for listeners to learn more about you. And so with that, Wes, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 韦斯，多年来我通过多种方式从你身上学到了很多东西——无论是在构建我的课程过程中，还是通过你的文章和推文。总之，你就是个超级迷人的人，我很高兴有这个机会能更多地了解你，也让听众能更好地认识你。所以，韦斯，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Hey, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 嘿，莱尼。很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my pleasure. So just to set a little context about the Wes that we know today, your career path has been pretty untraditional for many of the guests that we've had on this podcast. And so I'd love to just hear a brief, high level overview of your career and understand what made Wes the Wes that she is today.
turns.zh: 不客气。先简单介绍一下我们今天要聊的韦斯吧。与我们播客邀请的许多嘉宾相比，你的职业道路相当非传统。我很想听你简要概述一下职业生涯，了解是什么造就了今天的韦斯。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I started my career in corporate retail at the Gap headquarters in San Francisco. So I did a rotational training program, rotating between Old Navy, Banana Republic, Gap, and it was a great foundation in business fundamentals.
turns.zh: 我的职业生涯始于旧金山盖璞总部的零售业务。我参加了一个轮岗培训项目，在Old Navy、Banana Republic和盖璞之间轮换，这为我奠定了扎实的商业基础。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: A lot of people talk about, should I out of school go to a bigger company, or should I go to a startup? So I went to a bigger company and gradually have gone to smaller companies since then until finally starting my own in the past 15 years.
turns.zh: 很多人会纠结是毕业后去大公司还是创业公司。所以我选择了大公司，之后逐渐转向小公司，最终在过去15年里创立了自己的公司。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So I think that getting to see inside what a company that's been around for 40 plus years was like was really, really fantastic training and set me up for success for jumping into tech and other roles since then.
turns.zh: 我认为深入了解一家拥有40多年历史的公司的内部运作，是为我之后投身科技和其他领域奠定成功基础的绝佳培训。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: After Gap, I went to a beauty company that was acquired by Shiseido and then was at an ad tech company that was acquired by Snap. And then moved cross country from SF to New York to work with bestselling author, Seth Godin.
turns.zh: 离开盖璞后，我加入了一家被资生堂收购的美容公司，随后又进入一家被Snap收购的广告科技公司。之后我从旧金山搬到纽约，与畅销书作家赛斯·戈丁共事。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And that just changed my trajectory completely. It was just such a transformative experience getting to learn and work directly with for three years, one of the best marketing minds and just most creative minds, I think on the planet right now.
turns.zh: 这彻底改变了我的职业轨迹。能与赛斯直接学习并共事三年，与当今地球上最具创意的营销人才之一合作，这是一次极具变革性的经历。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And together we co-founded the altMBA, which I grew from just an idea between me and Seth, to thousands of students, 45 countries, 500 cities, grew our team from just us two to 60 plus people all over the world. So it was just an amazing, amazing experience.
turns.zh: 我们共同创立了altMBA项目。我把它从我和赛斯的构想，发展到吸引了来自45个国家、500个城市的数千名学生。我们的团队也从最初的两人扩展到全球60多人。整个过程堪称奇迹。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And then after that, I consulted for a couple of years working directly with other course creators who wanted to create their mini versions of the altMBA, and from doing that, really proved out the idea that the format of cohort-based courses was something that was really special, that other experts in other industries, other functions could really leverage.
turns.zh: 之后，我做了几年的顾问，直接与其他想打造迷你版altMBA课程的创作者合作。通过这段经历，我真正验证了基于小组学习的课程模式具有独特价值——其他行业、不同职能的专家都能借力这种模式。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And then that led to starting Maven because when I was consulting and when I was doing altMBA, during those six, seven years, I realized how janky the tech stack was that everyone was using. And I was shocked that no one had tackled this problem of all of us course creators needing to toggle between half a dozen different tools just to make a live plus async course be able to work.
turns.zh: 这促使我创立了Maven平台。因为在做顾问和开发altMBA课程的六七年间，我意识到当时人们使用的技术栈效率低下，令人不堪。令我震惊的是，没有人解决过这个问题——我们这些课程创作者每周都要在六七个不同的工具间切换，才能让直播和异步课程正常运作。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so when my co-founder Gagan Biyani and I got together, we were brainstorming what's the future of education and catching up. And we were just shocked that, hey, why hasn't anyone tackled this yet? We should do this because we both really believe that cohort-based courses are the future that [inaudible 00:07:02] want to teach these courses, but it's just too hard from a technical perspective now, but it doesn't have to be that way.
turns.zh: 于是，当我的联合创始人Gagan Biyani和我坐下来头脑风暴时，我们探讨了教育的未来，并交流近况。我们不禁惊呼：为什么没人解决这个问题？我们应该行动起来，因为我们深信基于小组学习的课程模式是未来的趋势。（不确定原文中的[inaudible 00:07:02]是什么，可能需要根据上下文补充）我们都坚信这种模式是未来的方向，但从技术角度来看目前存在太多障碍——但情况本不必如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I definitely want to chat a bit about Seth Godin. I've been such a huge fan of his for, I don't know, a decade. I used to subscribe to his newsletter and I don't anymore, because it's an email every day and it's overwhelming, even though he pointed out in one of his newsletters, okay, just ignore it. Why would you be sad that I have so much content? But yeah, anyway I unsubscribed recently, but I'm such a fan. And so I'm so curious, one, how did you connect with him and how did that even happen? And then two, what is he like to work with?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我绝对想聊聊塞斯·戈丁。我是他十年的忠实粉丝了。我曾订阅他的新闻通讯，但后来取消了订阅，因为每天邮件太多太烦人。尽管他在一封通讯中提到，嘿，别理会这些内容。我又有什么好难过的呢？但最近我还是取消了订阅，不过我确实是他的粉丝。所以我很好奇，一、你是如何与他结缘的？二、和他合作是什么样的体验？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Both very, very juicy questions. So the way that we connected was Seth had put out a blog post saying that he was looking for a special projects lead to help him figure out what to do next. So this was in 2014 when he had just sold off his last company Squidoo that he had been working on for I think, eight years or so before that.
turns.zh: 这两个问题都非常有趣。我们结缘的方式是，塞斯在2014年发布了一篇博文，称他正在寻找一位特别项目负责人来帮他规划下一步。当时他刚刚出售了自己经营了八年的公司Squidoo。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So he was ready for something new, at a crossroads, wanted some fresh inspiration, and I saw this blog post on a whim. And at that time I was at that ad tech company in San Francisco and I thought there are probably thousands of people who are going to be applying to this, so I don't want to get my hopes up. I did want to move to New York. I feel like everyone in SF and California at some time wants to move to New York. And so I thought, all right, I'm going to toss my hat in the ring and not overthink it.
turns.zh: 他准备迎接新挑战，处于人生的十字路口，渴望获得新的灵感。我偶然看到了这篇博文，当时我在旧金山的广告科技公司工作，觉得肯定有成千上万的人会申请这个职位，所以我没抱太大希望。但我确实想去纽约发展——感觉旧金山和加州的人都曾有过想去纽约的时刻。于是我决定试试运气，不想太多。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so the application required a video, so there was a written application and then there was a video. So Seth said, "Take three minutes to talk about what you want to build, what you want to contribute, and what you want to learn," something along those lines.
turns.zh: 申请流程需要提交视频，所以除了书面申请还需要一段视频。塞斯要求：“用三分钟时间谈谈你想打造什么样的产品、能贡献什么、想学习什么。”大致是这样的内容。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And I did my video in one take. Normally I would've done multiple takes for sure, but here I just thought there's a very little chance I'm going to get this. And a couple days later to my surprise, I get an email from Seth Godin. He's in my inbox and I'm just jumping up and down in my living room because he's asked, "Hey, loved your video. Let's hop on a call for an interview." And of course I write a very calm professional response and we did a couple rounds of interviews and I get the role.
turns.zh: 我的视频是一次性完成的。通常情况下，我肯定会多次拍摄，但这次我觉得成功的机会微乎其微。几天后，令我惊喜的是，赛斯·高丁发来邮件。他出现在我的收件箱里，我在客厅里兴奋得跳来跳去，因为他写道："嘿，喜欢你的视频。咱们约个时间聊聊吧。"我当然回复了一封从容专业的邮件，之后我们进行了几轮采访，最终我拿下了这个职位。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So I pack my life into six suitcases, get an apartment sight unseen in this little town right outside of New York City, where Seth's office is, it's called Hastings-on-Hudson. And what initially started off as a six month role eventually led to over three years working together and starting the altMBA together.
turns.zh: 于是，我把生活装进六个行李箱，毫不犹豫地搬到了纽约市外的小镇哈斯廷斯-昂-哈德逊（Hastings-on-Hudson），赛斯的办公室就位于那里。最初为期六个月的合作，最终演变成了三年多的共事，并共同创办了altMBA项目。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So that's how we got connected, very serendipitous. But my lesson there is don't take yourself out of the running before you get rejected. Don't reject yourself, basically. I think a lot of us have high standards and high expectations of ourselves and it's almost like, oh, if I can't do the best application, then I just shouldn't apply. If I don't have time to take five takes of this video, it won't be good enough, and so I just shouldn't do it. So for me, that was a great lesson in putting your best foot forward, but putting your foot forward.
turns.zh: 我们的缘分就这样开始了，充满了意外。但我从中得到的启发是：在被拒绝之前，别轻易否定自己。别自我设限。我觉得很多人对自己要求太高、期望太大，总会想："如果我的申请材料不够完美，就不该申请。""如果我没时间拍摄五个版本的视频，那它肯定不够好，所以干脆别拍了。"对我而言，这是一个重要的教训：要尽全力，但也要勇于迈出第一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这种状态。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So that was how we got connected. And then in terms of what it was like working with him, I think the Seth that people know externally can sometimes be different from the behind-the-scenes Seth. And that I think that's true for all of us, by the way. And so I think externally, he can sometimes be a little bit of a vague Buddha, if you will. He gives great inspiring advice. His insights, I think are amazing.
turns.zh: 就这样，我们建立了联系。说到和他共事的感受，我觉得外界熟知的赛斯和幕后真实的赛斯有时不太一样。顺便说一句，我觉得我们所有人都是如此。所以在公众视野里，他有时可能像个深藏不露的佛像，偶尔给出振聋发聩的建议，他的洞察力简直令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: If you look at his blog, some people try to copy Seth's blog by writing short daily posts, but that is not the reason why Seth's blog is so good. That is incidental, that they are short and daily. The reason why it works is because they are so insight rich.
turns.zh: 如果你看他的博客，就会发现有些人试图模仿他的写作风格，写些简短的日记式文章，但这并非他博客成功的秘诀。简短日更只是表象，真正的原因在于其深刻的洞察力。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And in person, he is even smarter and even sharper than he is in writing and online, which is so amazing. I'm just shocked by that because I feel like most people are the opposite. It's like you have time to curate what goes on your Twitter, your website. You have time to manicure this, what you want people to think of you, but when you are live, you're there with the person, you're talking like normal people and you can really get a sense of how sharp or insightful or genuine someone is. And I think he's even more genuine, even sharper, even funnier in person.
turns.zh: 而现实中，他比博客和网络形象更聪明、更敏锐，这太令人惊叹了。这让我很震惊，因为大多数人恰恰相反。他们有时间精心雕琢社交媒体内容，塑造理想人设，但面对面交流时，你会发现他的真面目——机智、深刻、风趣得多。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So that was kind of high level. I think the other thing is that internally we had really high standards for what we would ship, which is a little bit different, I think, than what you might think if you were a Seth reader. Because before I would read him and just do it, essentially, ship, put yourself out there, don't overthink it.
turns.zh: 以上只是大致感受。另外值得一提的是，我们内部对产品质量有着极高标准，这和普通读者想象的可能大相径庭。因为过去我读完赛斯的文章后，往往直接上线，不做过多深思熟虑。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And you might think that, that means that there's a trade-off with quality, but the thing that I found so surprising about working together was that we often produced work almost always that was high quality, fast, and what's that third thing of that triangle? Cheap, or not cheap, but affordable or economical. Usually it's like, oh, you only get two of these or there's the trade-off between quality and speed, but we worked fast and we produced really great work.
turns.zh: 你或许会认为这会牺牲质量，但合作过程中最让我惊喜的是，我们往往能产出高质量、快速完成的作品。质量、速度、成本——这三者通常存在权衡，但我们既保证了速度又做出了优质内容。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so I think for me, it really raised the bar on everything for me and on strategies, on tactics, on expectations, on quality, speed. I think the speed that we shipped ... Before I was at a Sequoia-backed ad tech startup and I thought, oh, I know what shipping fast is, I was at a startup.
turns.zh: 这段经历极大提升了我的标准——策略、战术、期望、质量、速度。赛斯团队的速度之快令人惊叹，远超我之前在红杉资本支持的广告科技初创公司所经历的。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And the speed that we shipped at Seth HQ was just beyond. It just blew away what I think normal people think of as fast, but it was also still so good. And so I think that rigor and that refusal to accept anything but excellence was just so awesome. And it really spoke to me because I care a lot about craft. I think more people should care about craft and I'm also kind of an obsessed person. I have an obsessive personality and I just loved how Seth was similarly obsessed. And so yeah, learned so much from him that I've taken with me obviously in building Maven now and everything that I do.
turns.zh: 赛斯总部的效率更是超乎想象。人们眼中的“快速”在这里被彻底重构，但质量依然出色。这种对卓越的执着追求让我深受触动，因为我深知精益求精的重要性。我希望更多人能重视工艺，我自己也是个痴迷于细节的人，而赛斯同样如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I've 10 more questions I'd love to ask about Seth Godin, but I should probably try to get him on the podcast. What a coup that would be. I have a sad story actually. I just remembered while you were talking, I saw him mentioned once that he replies to every email he gets. And so I emailed him because-
turns.zh: 哇。我还有10个关于赛斯·戈丁的问题想问，但我或许该设法请他上播客了。那可真是件大功劳。说实话，我有个尴尬的故事。刚才你讲的时候，我突然想起曾看到有人提到他会回复收到的每封邮件。于是我给他发邮件想确认——

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Just to check.
turns.zh: 结果他回复说："如果我不这么做，又有什么好处呢？"我当时就想，天啊，我把他惹毛了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... I had such a crush. Yeah, just to test. And he replied and he's like, "Why would I say this if I wasn't doing this? What benefit would that be for me?" I was like, "Oh shit, I pissed him off.
turns.zh: ……我当时可真是着了迷。是啊，就想测试一下。结果他回复说："如果我不这么做，又有什么好处呢？"我当时就想，天啊，我把他惹毛了。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So funny.
turns.zh: 太搞笑了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He hates me.
turns.zh: 他讨厌我。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: It's hilarious.
turns.zh: 真是太搞笑了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Okay. Amazing. One last quick question. You also worked with Scott Galloway, who's a very polarizing figure on Twitter at least, and you helped him create his courses. Maybe just one quick question on him, what's he like and why do people dislike him so much on Twitter?
turns.zh: 天啊。好吧。太棒了。最后再快速问一个问题。你还和斯科特·加洛韦合作过，他在推特上可是个极具争议的人物，至少在推特上是这样的。你帮他设计了课程。或许就快速问一下他吧，他是什么样的人？为什么人们在推特上这么不喜欢他？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yeah, I don't know about people disliking him. He definitely has spiky points of view, which I think are amazing. Yeah. So Section4, Scott Galloway's company was one of the first clients that I worked with after leaving altMBA, and I didn't work too closely with Scott. I worked really closely with his CEO, Greg Shove and their exec team to design the sprint that's now their go-to course format. But yeah, I didn't work too closely with him directly.
turns.zh: 是啊，我不知道人们为什么不喜欢他。他确实有一些尖锐的观点，我觉得这些观点很棒。是的。第四部分，斯科特·加洛韦的公司是我离开altMBA后合作的首批客户之一。我和斯科特本人合作不多，但我和他的首席执行官格雷格·肖夫以及高管团队密切合作，设计了现在成为他们主打课程模式的Sprint课程。不过我和他本人合作不多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. We won't get too deep there. Okay, so what I want to do with most of the time that we have together is to go into five big ideas. You could call it the five big ideas from Wes Kao, concepts that you've shared in other places that you've touched on your writing and tweeting and things like that have struck and have stuck with me and I suspect many other people, and just go deeper on these ideas. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 好的，没关系。我们就不深挖了。好的，我希望我们在一起的大部分时间能探讨五个核心观点。你可以称之为韦斯·考的五大理念——这些理念是你在其他地方分享过的，在你的写作、推特等内容中提及过的，对我以及其他许多人产生了深刻影响，现在我想更深入地探讨这些理念。这样听起来可以吗？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Sounds great.
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So the first idea I want to chat about is something you call the super specific how. And you wrote a post about this and it really clarified a lot of my thinking on writing and the newsletter and the podcast. And I find myself sharing this post and concept with other writers who are struggling a bit with their content. And so can you just explain this idea of the super specific how, and generally just how it can make folks better writers and thinkers?
turns.zh: 太好了。第一个我想聊的理念是你所谓的超级具体的how。关于这个你写了一篇文章，确实让我对写作、时事通讯和播客的很多思考都豁然开朗。我发现自己经常把这篇文章和这个理念分享给那些在内容创作上有些困惑的写作者。那么你能不能解释一下超级具体的how这个理念？总的来说，它如何能让人们成为更好的写作者和思考者？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yeah. The idea of the super specific how is that most writers, most course instructors spend too much time on the what and the why and not enough time on how. So if you think about people who are reading your writing, most of them probably already agree with the general premise of what you're saying.
turns.zh: 是的。超级具体的how的理念是，大多数作家和课程讲师在“是什么”和“为什么”上花费太多时间，而在“怎么做”上投入不足。想想正在阅读你作品的人，大多数人都已经认同你所说的基本观点了。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Unless what you're saying is truly controversial, a ground-breaker, or new to your audience, you don't need to spend too much time elaborating on the concept itself and why it matters. People really want to know how do I do this? How do I apply this to my own life? How do I think about the nuances when I'm applying this? What are examples that I can look at that help me better internalize how this really works?
turns.zh: 除非你说的是真正有争议、有开创性或者对听众来说全新的内容，否则你不需要花太多时间详细阐述概念本身及其重要性。人们真正想知道的是我该怎么做？我如何将这应用到自己的生活中？应用时要注意哪些细节？有哪些例子可以帮助我更好地理解它到底是如何运作的？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So a good example of this is if you're writing about product management and communication, let's say. So you don't want to spend too much time talking about how communication is important for product managers. Most product managers already know that. That's pretty 101, it's pretty basic.
turns.zh: 一个很好的例子是，比如你要写关于产品管理和沟通的内容。那么你不必花太多时间去讲沟通对产品经理的重要性——大多数产品经理都已经知道这一点。这太基础了，太老生常谈了。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Instead, you want to spend that time talking about how to get buy in when you don't have positional authority as a product manager, or how to turn chaos into order and be able to communicate effectively across multiple stakeholders, or how to communicate ideas where there're assertions and hypotheses that might not work, but you need to put something forward to get the team going. These are all elements of communication that are juicier and more specific than just saying, here's why communication is important.
turns.zh: 相反，你应该把时间花在探讨以下这些问题上：当你作为产品经理没有职位权威时，如何获得他人的认同；如何在混乱中建立秩序，并能与多方利益相关者有效沟通；或者当你的想法中存在可能行不通的假设和主张时，如何有效传达这些想法，以推动团队前进。这些沟通要素比简单地说"沟通很重要"更有价值、更具针对性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a lot of it is cutting the backstory basically and just get right to the meat of it.
turns.zh: 所以关键在于尽可能删减背景铺垫，直接切入核心内容。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ever since you wrote that, I'm like, this is why a lot of my writing seems to work because I try to cut the intro as much as possible and just get right to the meat of it.
turns.zh: 自从你写了那篇文章后，我就在想，这就是为什么我的很多文章效果不错的原因——因为我尽量减少开场白，直接切入重点。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I find sometimes in my writing, I'll write and then go back and cut a lot of the preamble. So most people need less context setting and preamble than you might think. And I have a framework that I call start right before you get eaten by the bear. And the idea is that if you're telling a story about camping, don't start talking about going to REI to buy a Patagonia jacket and then booking the campsite and the website had difficulties. And on the drive over, we stopped by this gas station.
turns.zh: 我发现有时候自己写作时，会先写下来，然后再回头删减大量前奏部分。大多数人需要的背景铺垫比你想象的要少。我有一个框架叫"在被熊吃掉前就开始行动"。意思是，如果你在讲一个露营的故事，别从去REI买巴塔哥尼亚夹克、预订露营地遇到网站故障、途中在加油站停留这些事说起。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: No one cares about all that. Start right before your friend left a Clif Bar out in their tent and you all almost got mauled by a bear. Get to the juicy part. And serve a little bit of context right before you get to the juicy part, but that's the idea of start right before you get eaten by the bear is cut out all that backstory scope creep.
turns.zh: 没人关心这些。直接从朋友把克利夫能量棒忘在帐篷里，结果差点被熊袭击开始讲起。在讲精彩部分前稍微补充点背景，但关键是"在被熊吃掉前就开始行动"的核心理念，就是要删减所有多余的背景铺垫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. There's also this element to your thinking that you didn't touch on, which is this, I think you call it the content hierarchy of bullshit.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个思路。你还有个没提到过的概念，叫"内容层级的胡说八道"。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you speak to that?
turns.zh: 能讲讲这个吗？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yeah. So if you imagine a pyramid, triangle, at the bottom, there's more room for BS, and at the very top of the triangle, there's less room for BS. So what's at the bottom of that triangle? Twitter, podcasts, short articles. It's basically situations that are one directional where people can't really challenge what you're saying. Keynote speech is another great one for lots of room for BS. So those are situations that they're more one directional.
turns.zh: 是的。所以如果你想象一个金字塔形的结构，底部是三角形，这里有更大的胡说八道的空间；而在三角形的顶部，胡说八道的空间就小得多了。那么这个三角形的底部是什么？Twitter、播客、短文。基本上都是单向交流的情境，人们无法真正挑战你所说的内容。主题演讲也是一个有很多胡说八道空间的好例子。所以这些都是单向交流的情境。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: With Twitter at least, it's 280 characters. It's something short that you're saying that's a little bit of a mic drop. You just say it, you leave it there, and then you get to walk away without needing to defend it, without needing to share your rationale or think about counter points, and so there's more room for BS, right? The format encourages or allows it. Let's say it allows it.
turns.zh: 至少Twitter的限制是280个字符。这是简短的表达，带点自以为是的感觉。你说完就离开，不需要为此辩护，也不需要分享你的理由或考虑反驳的观点，所以胡说八道的空间就更大了，对吧？这种形式本身就鼓励或允许这种情况。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: But as you move up the triangle of the content hierarchy of BS, there's less and less room for BS. So long form in-depth articles, less room for BS. You have to defend the idea, you have to convince your reader. Books, also less room for BS. And at the top of the triangle, courses, one directional courses like video courses on Udemy, LinkedIn Learning, but especially cohort-based courses where there is live and async interaction, there's very little room for BS.
turns.zh: 但当你沿着胡说八道内容层次的三角形向上移动时，胡说八道的空间就越来越小了。所以长篇深入的文章，胡说八道的空间就小了。你必须为你的观点辩护，必须说服读者。书籍同样如此，胡说八道的空间更小。而在三角形的顶部，课程，尤其是像Udemy、LinkedIn Learning这样的视频课程，尤其是基于群组的课程，实时和异步互动的，胡说八道的空间就非常小了。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So if you think about a webinar or a keynote talk or a book, you say the thing and that's it, but in a cohort-based course where your students are right there with you, where they can ask questions, when they can have conversation in the Zoom chat box, if you're saying something that doesn't really make sense, there could be a whole conversation happening in Zoom chat saying, "This doesn't make sense for X, Y, Z reasons." And so you have to be able to defend what it's that you're saying and make sure that what you're saying is rigorous.
turns.zh: 所以如果你想想网络研讨会、主题演讲或书籍，你说完就结束了，但在基于群组的课程中，你的学生就在你身边，他们可以提问，可以在Zoom聊天框里交流。如果你说了不合理的东西，Zoom聊天里可能就会展开讨论，"这在X、Y、Z方面不合理。"所以你必须能够为你所说的内容辩护，确保你所说的内容是严谨的。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And I think that thinking about that content hierarchy of BS is great for holding ourselves to a higher standard, to make sure that we are not allowing ourselves to spew BS, just because a format might allow it. A book, for example, obviously the content of that book, the contents matter more than just the format. And so there are books that could be 10 page blog posts, and there are books where every page earns its real estate. So there's still a little bit of nuance in the hierarchy, but in general, as you move up that hierarchy, there's less and less room for BS.
turns.zh: 我认为思考这种胡说八道的内容层次结构对于我们坚持更高的标准非常有用，确保我们不允许自己随意胡说八道，只因为某种形式可能允许这样做。例如，一本书，显然书的内容比形式更重要。因此，有些书可能只有10页的博客文章，而有些书的每一页都物有所值。所以这个层次结构中仍有一些细微差别，但总的来说，随着你向上移动层次，就越没有胡说八道的空间了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this framework explains a bit why Twitter's so cringe to a lot of people is these threads that just sounds so wise, but yeah, there's not a lot of depth to them if you really think about it and it's easy to sound smart.
turns.zh: 我认为这个框架很好地解释了为什么Twitter对很多人来说很尴尬——那些听起来很明智的帖子，但如果你仔细想想，其实没什么深度。也很容易让人觉得自己很聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one thing I'll add is people are listening and they may be like, "Oh, of course courses are at the top, Wes runs a course company." But having run a course and created a course, I 100% agree that there's just no room for BS in a course, because one, there's just so much content because there's so much time that you have to cover. And so you can't just like, "Here's a wise thought, let's move on." You have to actually get into it and people hold you accountable to that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 所以我要补充一点，人们可能会听了然后想，"哦，当然课程在顶部，韦斯经营着一家课程公司。"但作为一个经营过课程并创建过课程的人，我百分之百同意课程中没有胡说八道的空间，因为首先，内容太多了，因为你有太多时间需要覆盖。你不能只是说，"这里有个明智的想法，我们继续下一个。"你必须真正深入探讨，人们会追究你对这些内容的责任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then to your point, people are going to ask questions and you're like, "Oh, shit, that's all I got. I have nothing more to add." That's not going to cut it. And so I totally agree. And that's why courses I think are so powerful and probably a much better way to learn than just reading a blog post or listening to a podcast if you really want go deep on something. So I love that concept.
turns.zh: 接下来回到你的观点，当人们提问时，你可能会觉得：“天哪，我已经说完了。我没法再补充什么了。” 但这可不行。因此我完全赞同你的看法。这就是为什么我认为课程比单纯阅读博客文章或听播客更有效，如果你真的想深入探讨某个主题的话。所以我很喜欢这种模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anything else you want to add on that idea before we move on to the next concept?
turns.zh: 在我们转入下一个概念之前，你还有什么想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Let's go. Next concept.
turns.zh: 开始吧。下一个概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So when I was building my PM course with you, you blew my mind a number of times on how to actually teach effectively. And one of the lessons you taught me was around the importance of creating state change in the talk, how to create state change. And so without giving it away, I'd love to just hear your thoughts on what is state change, why is it important, and just, how does it help you, not only give better talks, but also even better Zoom meetings?
turns.zh: 好的。我和你们一起开发项目管理课程时，你在如何有效授课方面给了我很多启发。其中你教给我的一个方法是，如何在演讲中创造状态变化。现在我就不剧透太多了，但我很想听听你对状态变化的看法——它为何重要，又如何能帮助我们不仅提升演讲效果，甚至让Zoom会议更高效？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: If you think about most Zoom meetings or presentations, it's one person talking at you the entire time and everyone else has to listen silently. It's pretty hard to do that on Zoom where your camera's on, you're sitting, you have to sit still, look straight ahead at the camera, control your face and make sure you look focused. And so it's really not surprising that most people find that very draining. They want to turn off their cameras, they get distracted.
turns.zh: 回想大多数Zoom会议或演示，通常都是一个人自始至终在讲，所有人只能默默听着。这在Zoom上尤其困难——摄像头开着，你还得坐着不动，全神贯注地盯着镜头控制表情。难怪大多数人觉得这很疲惫。他们想关掉摄像头，分心走神。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So the idea behind what I call the state change method is that you should punctuate your monologues with state changes. So state changes are anything that shakes your audience awake and adds some variety. So it might be asking people to put something in the chat box. It might be switching from gallery view where you see everyone in that Brady Bunch grid and switch over to screen share, to share something and then switch back.
turns.zh: 我所说的"状态变化方法"核心在于，用各种方式打破单调的演讲节奏。状态变化可以是让听众保持专注的任何元素。比如让大家在聊天框输入内容，从全员可见的"画廊视图"切换到屏幕共享，分享内容后再切回画廊视图。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: It might be having someone else speak. It might be asking people to unmute themselves and go ahead and chime in. It might be putting people into breakout rooms, so they can discuss amongst themselves and then come back and then do a popcorn where someone shares out and they popcorn to the next person to the next person.
turns.zh: 也可以让其他人发言，让大家静音后积极参与，还能分组讨论，最后进行弹幕分享。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So all these are examples of state changes that help your audience stay engaged with the material that you are presenting. And it's really in reaction to monologues. I'm kind of imagining Salesforce with their no software sticker. If you think about no monologues, try to avoid monologues as much as possible because that puts your audience to sleep.
turns.zh: 这些都是让听众保持参与度的技巧，尤其适用于Zoom会议。正如Salesforce倡导的"无软件演示"理念——避免长篇大论，尽可能互动，让听众保持清醒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are examples of different states? You mentioned breakouts, chat. What other sorts of things can you do, especially on a Zoom let's say for running a meeting?
turns.zh: 不同状态的例子有哪些？你提到了分组讨论、Zoom聊天、从画廊视图切换到屏幕共享展示内容再切回。还有投票功能。在揭示某个内容前，可以先问大家："你们怎么看？" 让大家猜测。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So we talked about breakouts, Zoom chat, switching from gallery view into screen share to show something and walk through it and then switch back. There's polls. Before you reveal something, you can ask, what do you all think? Go ahead and guess.
turns.zh: 我们讨论了分组讨论、Zoom聊天、从画廊视图切换到屏幕共享展示内容再切回。还有投票功能。在揭示某个内容前，可以先问大家："你们怎么看？" 让大家猜测。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So in the Maven Course Accelerator, the two week course that I teach on how to build a cohort-based course, it's very meta, I will ask people, so what do you think the average attention span is for students? So I could have just told people it's X, but anytime, when you want to just share a piece of information, that's an opportunity for a potential state change.
turns.zh: 因此，在我教授的Maven课程加速器中——那是一个为期两周的关于如何打造基于社群的课程的课程——这是一个非常具有元性的环节。我会问大家，你们认为学生平均的注意力持续时间是多久？我本可以直接告诉大家答案，但每当你想分享一段信息时，这都是一个引发潜在状态转换的机会。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Have people guess. The more they engage and think about the problem themselves, the more that they are going to remember and also just interact with your material. So I ask people to guess, and then the answers range from an hour or 45 minutes to three seconds. So it's just all over the place. The answer's two to four minutes, according to some research. So that's a ripe opportunity for state change.
turns.zh: 让大家猜测。他们越是参与其中，自己思考这个问题，就越容易记住这些信息，也越容易与你的材料互动。所以我让大家猜测，答案从一小时、45分钟到三秒不等。但根据一些研究，正确答案应该是两到四分钟。这正是引发状态转换的绝佳机会。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And the other way to think about it, I was talking to Nathan Barry from ConvertKit, he was saying that he loves stage change method too, and that anytime he does a presentation now, every three to five slides, he'll put in a state change. So the idea of every three to five minutes, every three to five slides, go ahead and put in a stage change.
turns.zh: 还有另一种思考方式。我和ConvertKit的Nathan Barry聊过，他说他也非常喜欢这种状态转换的方法。现在每次他做演示时，每隔三到五张幻灯片，就会加入一个状态转换环节。所以每隔三到五分钟，每隔三到五张幻灯片，就应该加入一个状态转换环节。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: We really want to turn this from an art into a science, as much as possible, audience engagement. And if you just force yourself to look through your own material and say, "Oh, have I done a state change in the last couple of minutes?" If not, go ahead and throw one in. And more likely than not, when you look at that material at those intervals, you'll find something that lends itself really well to a state change.
turns.zh: 我们真的想尽可能地把这件事从艺术转化为科学，让观众参与进来。如果你强迫自己审视自己的材料，问自己：“哦，我在过去几分钟里有没有进行过状态转换？”如果没有，那就赶紧加入一个。很可能在你每隔几分钟审视一次材料时，你会发现一些非常适合引发状态转换的内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm feeling pressure to create some state change in this podcast. Hey listeners, when was the last time you were in a meeting where there was some meaningful state change? Think about that for a moment.
turns.zh: 我现在也感受到在这次播客中创造一些状态转换的压力。嘿，听众们，你们上次参加的会议中，有没有出现过有意义的状态转换？想一想吧。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Love it. Yes.
turns.zh: 太棒了。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. We're pros. Okay, I'm going to try to practice this lesson live. There's also this concept that you touch on, I think it's called eyes light up concept or something like that.
turns.zh: 好的。我们都是专业人士。好吧，我要试着在直播中实践这一课。你提到的这个概念，我觉得叫做“眼睛亮起来”的概念，或者类似的概念。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯-嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Can you speak to that, because I think it relates to this idea of state change in meetings?
turns.zh: 好的，很酷。你能详细说一下吗？因为我觉得这和会议中的状态转换理念有关。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yeah. So the idea behind what I call eyes lighting up is that when you're talking to someone and you're explaining something, you're teaching them, you're sharing your startup idea or whatever the normal response is people will want to be polite. So they'll nod and they'll say, "Oh, okay, that's interesting." But there's usually a moment in the conversation where their eyes light up because they are genuinely actually interested in what you are saying at that moment.
turns.zh: 是的。我所说的眼睛亮起来背后的理念是，当你和某人交谈，解释某件事，或者分享你的创业想法时，人们通常会出于礼貌而点头或说“哦，好的，这很有趣”。但在对话中通常会有一个时刻，他们的眼睛亮起来了，因为他们真的对你正在说的话感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So you, as the presenter, as the salesperson or whatever, that's pitching, you want to make note of the moments when people's eyes light up because their face can't lie. They can say, "Oh yeah. Okay, that's interesting." It's easy to say that and be polite, but when someone's eyes light up, that's a sign that something that you said triggered a reaction in them, a visceral reaction.
turns.zh: 所以作为演讲者、销售人员或者任何推销产品的人，你要留意人们眼睛亮起来的时刻，因为他们的表情不会说谎。他们可以说“哦，是的，好的，这很有趣”，但当有人眼睛亮起来时，这就是一个信号，表明你说的话在他们心中引发了某种反应，一种发自内心的反应。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And I think so many of us, we like to pretend that, oh, I don't get enough data from people and this person said this, but what do they really mean? And really I think that we're just being delusional. If we just acknowledge reality and this person looks bored, they look bored, that is data. Don't ignore that data. And then, oh wait there, I said this hot key word or this phrase or I explained something this way and all of a sudden, their face change or demeanor change, they're leaning forward, they're wanting to catch what you're saying, that's all data.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们很多人都喜欢假装自己没能从他人那里获得足够的信息——比如，“这人说了这番话，但他们到底什么意思呢？”但说实话，我们这不过是在自欺欺人。如果我们能正视现实——比如对方看起来无聊，面露不耐烦，这本身就是重要的信息。别忽视这些细节。再比如，当你提到某个关键词、短语或解释某个概念时，对方突然神情专注、身体前倾、全神贯注地听你讲话——这些都是宝贵的线索。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So really the principle behind eyes light up is don't be delusional in just taking people's, what they're saying at face value. Really look at their face, look for other clues, the excitement in their voice and watch for these different eyes light up moments, because those are great fodder for content that you might want to write about, for the angle of your sales pitch, for how you might want to explain something in the future. And you really cut out all the parts that make people go dead in the eyes and just say the parts that make their eyes light up.
turns.zh: 所以，“眼睛放光”背后的核心原则是：别被表象蒙蔽，别想当然地理解对方的字面意思。真正观察他们的面部表情，留意其他细节——比如声音中的兴奋感，以及那些眼睛放光的瞬间。这些都是创作优质内容、设计销售方案、未来解释事物的重要素材。同时，要摒弃那些让听众毫无反应的部分，只保留能激发他们兴趣的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hey listeners, what kind of eyes lighting up behaviors can you think of that show you somebody's really into your content?
turns.zh: 听众朋友们，你们还能想到哪些能显示对方对内容感兴趣的举动呢？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Or when are times in recent weeks when you've explained something or given a sales pitch and saw people's eyes light up? What were you saying in that moment? Think about that and jot that down.
turns.zh: 最近几周，当你向别人讲解某个概念或进行销售演示时，是否有过让对方眼睛放光的时刻？当时你在讲什么？不妨回想一下，把这些瞬间记录下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so the skill here is okay, for sales, that's interesting. So as a salesperson, it'll help you understand what part of your pitch resonates. I imagine for presentation prep, this is a useful skill. Obviously for building courses, probably less useful for meetings, but I imagine there's also just like, oh wow, this person got really excited when I share this thing, maybe spent a little more time on that idea.
turns.zh: 这项技能在销售中尤其实用，能帮助你了解哪部分内容最能引起共鸣。我想对于演示准备来说，这也是一项宝贵技能。显然对于课程开发可能用处不大，但对于会议来说同样适用。比如，内部会议、与跨职能团队成员、老板、直属下属的对话中，当你解释某个观点时，能明显感觉到他们的反应——比如“哦，对呀，就是这个”。或者某些部分引发了更高的热情。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I think it absolutely works for meetings. I think it works for internal meetings, for conversations, even with your cross-functional team members, with your boss, with your direct reports. Usually as you're explaining something, you can tell when even your manager is like, "Oh yeah, that." Or you can tell there's more energy in the response for certain parts.
turns.zh: 我认为这项技能在会议中同样适用，无论是内部会议、日常对话，甚至与跨职能团队成员、老板、直属下属的交流。通常在你解释某个观点时，能判断出甚至你的经理也会点头回应，或者某些部分引发了更强的兴趣。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And when you think about it, you can find patterns of, oh, usually, when I share things with this person, they tend to react well when I share these things. So why don't I trim out the other context that they don't really care about and focus on whatever made their eyes light up. And it might be talking about numbers, or it might be talking about upside, or it might be talking about how little effort this is to try. Whatever angle it is, it really gives you great data that you can lean into and flesh out more.
turns.zh: 仔细想想，你会发现规律——比如，当我向这个人分享某些内容时，他们往往反应良好。那么为什么不剔除他们不关心的其他背景信息，专注于能让他们眼睛放光的部分呢？无论是数据、优势，还是低成本尝试的可能性——无论哪个角度，这都能为你提供宝贵的信息，助你深入挖掘并充实内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned your manager and that's a really good segue to our next topic, which is around managing up.
turns.zh: 你提到了经理，这正是我们下一个话题的切入点——管理上级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If a feature ships, but no one knows about it, did it really ship? Keeping customers and internal teams like sales, support and marketing in the loop on what's changing across your product is surprisingly hard.
turns.zh: 如果某个功能上线了，但没人知道，那算真正上线了吗？让客户和内部团队（如销售、支持、市场）了解产品变化的进展，出乎意料地困难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First you have to dig through tickets and pull requests just to see what's been done. Then you have to figure out what's relevant to each person, craft updates, and then share them across all of your channels. Multiply this by the number of things that ship every week and that's basically a full-time job just to keep everyone updated on what's changing. That's why high velocity product teams like Monte Carlo, Armory and PopSQL use Makelog.
turns.zh: 首先，你得在海量的工作项和提拉请求中翻找，才能了解已完成的工作。然后，你得梳理出与每个人相关的信息，撰写更新内容，再通过各种渠道分享这些信息。若将每周上线的新功能数量乘以这个过程，光是让所有人及时了解变化就足以成为一项全职工作。正因如此，Makelog等高效产品团队如Monte Carlo、Armory和PopSQL才选择了它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makelog makes it easy to see what's happening across tools like Jira, Linear, Asana, and GitHub, and then to write bite-sized updates, which you can immediately share with your audience wherever they are, including within your app, on Slack, over email, and even on Twitter. No more long boring blog style change log posts that slow you down, just quick and easy updates that keep your users informed and happy. Try, Makelog for free today. Just visit, makelog.com/lenny to get started.
turns.zh: Makelog能轻松整合Jira、Linear、Asana和GitHub等工具的信息，生成简洁易懂的更新内容，随时随地与受众分享——无论是在应用内、Slack、邮件还是Twitter上。无需再撰写冗长乏味、拖慢进度的博客式变更日志，只需快速简洁地更新，让用户及时知晓动态，提升满意度。立即免费试用Makelog，请访问makelog.com/lenny即可开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think your most popular tweet you've ever tweeted is around the skill of managing up. And funny enough, I had a thread on managing up years ago and it's also my most popular tweet thread ever. So there's a lot of interest in this topic. And so I want to ask you why is managing up important? Why are people not doing it well and how do you manage up effectively?
turns.zh: 我记得你最火的推文是关于“向上管理”的技巧。说来有趣，我多年前也写过一篇关于向上管理的推文，那也是我最受欢迎的推文主题。可见这个话题备受关注。接下来我想问你，向上管理为何如此重要？为何人们做得不好，又该如何有效做到向上管理？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Great questions. I think that most people assume that their boss has to manage them and they feel a little bit resentful that, why should I manage my boss? They're getting paid more. They are my manager. They have more responsibility. And you can continue to think that way and your career might be fine, but if you embrace that, if you manage your boss, they're going to appreciate you much more, you're going to get more opportunities, you're going to have more trust with them, there's all these great things that happen when you decide to manage up.
turns.zh: 这些问题很棒。我认为大多数人默认应该由老板来管理自己，心存不满地想：凭什么要我管理老板？他们挣得更多，又是我的上司，责任更重。这种想法或许能维持现状，但若主动向上管理，效果会截然不同。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And I think more people are realizing that, hey, as an individual contributor, or even as a manager, we all have bosses. So even as someone who leads people, you still need to manage up. There's no point in seniority where, as you climb the career ladder, that it just doesn't matter anymore.
turns.zh: 越来越多人意识到，嘿，作为个体贡献者，甚至管理者，我们都有上司。即便身为领导者，也需向上管理。职级越高，越不意味着这种需求消失。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And I think some people think that senior people don't need to manage up like, oh, once I'm a director of VP, I don't need to manage up anymore, it's only something I need to do when I'm a coordinator or an associate PM or something. But ironically, the most senior people are best at managing up. This is why they got promoted in the first place because they were great at managing up to their bosses to understand what was worrying their bosses, what was keeping them up at night so that they could take that off their plate.
turns.zh: 有些人认为高管无需向上管理，认为一旦升任总监或副总裁，就无需再管了。但讽刺的是，最资深的人往往最擅长向上管理。这正是他们晋升的根本原因——因为他们善于向上沟通，理解老板的担忧，分担压力。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: They're great at keeping their bosses in the loop on what's happening so their bosses, aren't constantly having to ask and pepper them with questions every day on, hey, how's this going? Or what's the status of this? Or do we take care of this thing? They're proactive in communicating so their boss knows that certain things are taken care of. And so there's so many benefits that you can reap when you choose to manage up.
turns.zh: 他们主动汇报进度，避免老板每天追问“进展如何？”“状态如何？”“这事儿办好了吗？”这种主动沟通让上司安心，无需时刻催促。选择向上管理能带来诸多益处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you suggest folks do it? I actually have a tip, but is there something you want to share in that?
turns.zh: 你建议人们如何做到这一点？我倒有个小技巧，但你是否也有心得想分享？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yeah. I think one really big way of doing that is keeping your boss in the loop on the kinds of decisions that you're making and what you are working on. It feels almost blase like, well, duh, but actually I think we all know that we should do that, but the way that we execute, I think sometimes your boss doesn't feel like they're in the loop. And so proactively giving the right amount of context for your manager to be able to weigh in on what you're doing and to be able to give feedback, I think that's super, super important.
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为要做到这一点，关键在于让你的上司随时了解你正在做出的决策和正在推进的工作。听起来这似乎是理所当然的，但实际上我觉得我们都知道应该这么做，但执行起来却常常让上司感觉被蒙在鼓里。所以主动为经理提供足够的背景信息，让他们能对你的工作进行评估并提供反馈，这一点非常重要。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And then thinking about the right level of context to give them, is this a reversible decision or is this one that is irreversible or difficult to reverse or expensive to reverse? Using your sense of judgment so that you're not necessarily going to your boss for everything and telling them everything. That's overwhelming for your manager who has a lot going on, it's really using your sense of judgment and good common sense to think about, okay, I want to recommend that we do this thing. How do I share enough context about my thought process and rationale so that my boss has enough information to be able to push back if needed or to be able to approve and know that I've gotten it taken care of?
turns.zh: 然后要考虑提供多少背景信息才是合适的。这是个可逆的决策，还是不可逆、难以撤销或代价高昂的决策？要运用自己的判断力，不必事事都向上司汇报。毕竟上司的日常事务繁忙，关键在于运用判断力和常识，思考好：我想推荐我们做这件事。我该如何充分传达我的思考过程和逻辑，让上司能在必要时提出异议，或是批准并放心交由我处理？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So to build on that, something I did for a long time, that was really powerful, it's really simple is I sent my manager a state of Lenny email every week, just titled the state of Lenny. And it had basically three sections, my priorities currently, blockers that I need their help with, and maybe that was the first thing that I put up just to make sure that they saw that, and then just things on my mind currently that week.
turns.zh: 太棒了。基于这个经验，我曾长期采用一个简单却有效的方法：每周给经理发一封名为《Lenny近况》的邮件。邮件主要分三个部分：我当前的优先事项、需要他们协助解决的障碍（这可能是我最先列出的内容，确保他们能第一时间看到），以及当周我正在思考的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that I think is such a simple, but such a powerful way to do exactly what you're talking about, keep people in the loop about what you're doing, make sure you're aligned on priorities, make sure things are getting unblocked, and also just avoid surprise as much as possible. And so there's a little tip.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个简单却强大的方法，能完美实现你所说的目标——让大家随时了解你的工作进展，确保优先事项达成共识，及时解决障碍，并尽可能避免突发状况。这里有个小技巧。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I love that. I think the avoiding surprises is great. I think in the work context, surprises are generally not great. So I always say, unless you're surprising me by bringing me a snack or something, don't surprise me. Actually, in my personal life too, I don't like surprises. So I think, especially in work, not throwing something over to your manager that just catches them off guard is good.
turns.zh: 我很赞同。避免突发状况很重要。在工作环境中，意外通常不是好事。正如我常说的，除非你给我带零食之类的惊喜，否则别让我意外。其实在个人生活中，我也不喜欢惊喜。所以我觉得，尤其是在工作中，别给上司带来措手不及的惊喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that general rule, avoid surprises, except for birthday parties and milestones. That also touches on just a general rule I have of working is just over communicate. I find nobody's ever like, "Just, Lenny, shut up. I don't want to know about things." It's always the opposite, why didn't I know about this? Even if they don't pay attention, the fact that they have the chance to see it always goes a long way.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个通用规则：避免突发状况，除非是生日派对或里程碑事件。这也与我的一项工作准则相契合——多沟通。事实上，没人会说：“闭嘴，Lenny，我不想知道这些事。”相反，他们总会问：“你怎么不早说？”即使他们没注意到，至少有机会了解情况，这就很有帮助了。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I find especially in remote work too erring on the side of over communicating is just, it ends up being the right level of communication. You think you're over communicating, but to the recipient, it's actually just the right amount. And I've been surprised by how I thought everyone was aligned on a certain strategy or that, oh, we've already talked about this thing three times and then realized that, oh, we actually weren't as aligned as I thought.
turns.zh: 尤其是在远程工作中，我发现多沟通反而恰到好处。最终证明，这才是合适的沟通频率。你以为自己沟通过度了，但对收件人而言，恰恰是刚刚好的量。我曾惊讶地发现，自己以为大家对某项策略达成一致，结果却发现根本不一致。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So erring on side of over communication is great. And I think also structuring your communication in a way where if someone already agrees with you or they get it, they can get the gist, but if someone doesn't get it, they can continue reading. So that helps people spend their time well.
turns.zh: 因此，适当多传达一些信息并没有什么坏处。我认为，还可以这样安排沟通内容：如果对方已经认同你的观点或理解了你的意思，他们能领会大意；但如果对方不明白，你可以继续解释。这能帮助人们有效利用时间。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So I'll usually put the most important point at the top, the TLDR, if you will, the gist and then I'll say context, colon, and then that there might be multiple paragraphs of context below for anyone who wants additional thinking on how did I get to this decision, or how did I think about this. But if they already agree with the decision and know that context, then they don't need to keep reading.
turns.zh: 所以我通常会先把最重要的观点放在最上面，用术语来说就是TLDR（太长不看），简要概括关键内容，然后再说明背景，冒号开头，接着可能会有几段背景说明，供有兴趣深入探讨决策过程或思考逻辑的人阅读。但如果对方已经认同你的决定并了解背景，就没必要继续往下读了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually taught that format in my course. I think it was rooted in the military where they're just like, their emails start with bottom line, here's what you need to know, and then context, bullet point, bullet point, bullet point, bullet point. And so it's a really simple way of just communicating things.
turns.zh: 我在课程中确实教过这种格式。这种方式源自军方，他们的邮件通常开头就是“核心观点”，然后是关键信息，再是背景说明，用项目符号列出要点。这种简洁明了的沟通方式非常高效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Although one student used that format with a potential customer where they started off being bottom line, here's where we're at and they were like, "Man, that's aggressive." And so I had to adjust that to be a little softer. Okay.
turns.zh: 不过有个学生用这种格式给潜在客户发邮件，开头就是“核心观点”，直接说我们目前的进展，结果对方反应说：“天哪，这也太强硬了吧。”所以我不得不调整语气，让沟通更温和一些。好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I had this beautiful segue, but anyway, you talked about communication and that's a good segue to talking about writing and you have a lot of great advice on writing and how to write well. We touched on a bit of this, of cutting out the backstory and being super specific with the how, but do you have any other advice for just writing in general? Because a lot of folks that listen to this are trying to write more and you have some great stuff on this. So yeah, what can you share?
turns.zh: 我提到了沟通技巧，现在来谈谈写作吧。你对写作有很多宝贵建议，比如去掉背景故事，专注于如何传达信息。但听众中很多人想提高写作水平，你能否再分享一些通用技巧？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I think a lot of people learn writing from mimicking other people and learning by analogy, especially on Twitter or on social, which I think is useful to a certain point, but I also think that there's a lot of benefit in studying the craft of writing off of social. So one of the books that I've been recommending, I think I'm jumping ahead to potentially a lightning round question, but-
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人通过模仿他人或类比学习写作，比如在推特或社交媒体上，但这种方法效果有限。更重要的是，要系统学习写作技巧。比如我推荐的书《It Was the Best of Sentences, It Was the Worst of Sentences》，作者是June Casagrande，书名翻译成《句子的最佳与最差》。我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。还有《Better Business Writing》，哈佛商学院出版社出版的系列书籍，涵盖领导力、上级管理、写作等内容。我通常会把这两本书推荐给新加入的团队成员，因为它们更侧重于如何打造有力的句子、段落、论点，以及思考逻辑的连贯性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not allowed.
turns.zh: 不允许。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: ... it's a book called It Was the Best of Sentences, It Was the Worst of Sentences by June Casagrande, I think is her name. So we'll link this in the show notes. And another one is Better Business Writing by Harvard Business Press. They have a whole series on leadership, managing up, writing, et cetera. And I recommend those two books usually to new team members who join because they cover more of the craft of creating strong sentences, paragraphs, arguments and thinking about the logic of what you're saying.
turns.zh: ... 推荐的书有June Casagrande的《It Was the Best of Sentences, It Was the Worst of Sentences》，以及哈佛商学院出版社的《Better Business Writing》。它们涵盖领导力、上级管理、写作等系列内容。我通常会把这两本书推荐给新加入的团队成员，因为它们更侧重于如何打造有力的句子、段落、论点，以及思考逻辑的连贯性。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: A lot of times when we write a sentence, there's actually already a point of view or there's a point of view baked in, but you don't want it to be an accidental point of view. I was just talking to my team member about this, she asked me to give her some feedback on something that she wrote and the way that she had written her paragraph was leading for the reader.
turns.zh: 很多时候，我们写句子时已经带有某种观点或暗含某种立场，但你不希望这种观点是无意中产生的。我刚和团队成员讨论了这个问题，她让我给她反馈她写的段落，发现她的段落结构引导着读者。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: It was about an offsite that we have coming up and she talked about whether we should change a WeWork location, something like that. So this is actually super useful, tactical stuff for Slack messages, if you're DMing someone, if you're texting someone, you can use these principles basically everywhere.
turns.zh: 当时我们即将举办一场场外活动，她提到了是否要更换WeWork的办公地点之类的问题。其实这些内容对Slack消息来说非常实用——无论是私信某人，还是给别人发短信，都能应用这些技巧。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so it was a Slack message about changing WeWork locations and the way that she had phrased it, the obvious conclusion was, oh, well, we should just stick with our current one. And so I asked her, is that your recommendation? Because if it is then great, because you're leading the reader to that conclusion. But if it's not, you're asking a leading question that is skewing the results of this question.
turns.zh: 那次Slack消息是关于是否要更换WeWork办公地点的，而她表述的方式明显暗示着我们应该继续使用现有的办公地点。于是我问她："这是你的建议吗？" 因为如果是的话，那很棒，因为你这样引导读者得出这个结论。但如果不是，那你就是在提出一个引导性问题，会影响问题的客观性。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so it turned out that she was open. She didn't really have an opinion. And so we thought, okay, how do we adjust this so that it'll get a more objective response? And then we talked about it some more and thought it's actually better, if you do share a recommendation here, it's easier for the reader. So how do we then adjust it some more so that the recommendation is intentional within that paragraph?
turns.zh: 结果发现她持开放态度，并没有明确的意见。于是我们思考如何调整，让回答更客观。经过进一步讨论，我们意识到如果直接分享建议，读者会更容易理解。所以如何在段落中更自然地植入建议呢？

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I know it's not quite a soundbite, but I see this a lot in people's writing is that there's these either sentence structures that add more cognitive load to the reader or have a little bit of confusion, and it's a technical issue actually. It's like the which or some clause explains something directly before it, but they actually meant for that clause to describe something 10 words before at the beginning of the sentence, right?
turns.zh: 我知道这不算一个简洁的观点，但我在很多人的写作中发现，有些句子结构会增加读者的认知负担，或者造成理解困惑。这其实是个技术问题。比如，"which"或"some"从句需要在直接解释的内容前补充前置信息，但作者却想让前置从句描述句首十个词前的内容。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: It's hard without a visual, but anyway, both of those books talk about the mechanics and the technical aspects of writing and the craft of writing really well. And I guess my spiky point of view is that more people should learn the craft of writing and the technical aspects of writing, not just look at what other people are doing to try to get audience engagement, but to actually improve your ability to precisely say what you mean and convey the level of conviction that you have and not accidentally mislead people with your words, because you didn't know that the way you wrote something could potentially mislead them.
turns.zh: 没有视觉示例可能有点难理解。不过这两本书都很好地讲解了写作的技巧和机制。我想我比较尖锐的观点是，更多人应该学习写作技巧和写作技术，而不是模仿他人的做法来吸引读者，而是真正提高自己准确传达意图和信念的能力，同时避免用词误导他人，因为你可能不知道自己的表达方式会让读者产生误解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. I actually got that same feedback that you gave this person once when I clearly had an opinion on what we should do as a team, and I gave pros and cons and it was very biased and clear what I thought we should do. And my manager's like, "Don't do that. Just try to be as unbiased as you can or just tell me here's what you think we should do, and here's why." And it helped a lot.
turns.zh: 明白了。我其实也遇到过类似的情况，有次我明确表达了团队应该怎么做，列举了利弊，态度很明显。但我的经理说："别这样。尽量保持中立，或者直接告诉我你认为该怎么做，以及原因。"这对我帮助很大。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I love that. And I think pulling on the thread a little bit it's because pros and cons lists, the structure of a pro and con list implies that you are giving equal weight to pros and cons, that you are accurately talking about pros and cons or objectively talking about them.
turns.zh: 我很赞同这一点。再深入思考一下，之所以会这样，是因为利弊列表的结构暗示着你对利弊给予了同等重视，即你准确地讨论了利弊，或者客观地陈述了利弊。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So when you do a pros and cons list, but they're skewed and you are leaving some things out of the cons list, it makes the reader suspicious and they can't trust you anymore, whereas if you do a pros and cons list, but at the top, you say my recommendation is X, here's pros and cons of that, or here's some risks associated with it or whatever, you're building trust with your reader because you were direct in saying, "Here's my recommendation, here's what I'm advocating for. And also, here are some downsides to that."
turns.zh: 因此，当你列出利弊清单时，如果信息有偏差，或者遗漏了某些弊端，这会让读者产生怀疑，进而失去对你的信任。相反，如果你先给出自己的推荐，再列出利弊，或者说明相关风险，这就能建立起读者的信任，因为你坦率地表明了自己的立场：“这是我的建议，接下来是利弊分析，以及可能存在的风险。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. This also reminds me of the mental pyramid, which I won't get too deep into, but the concept there is in business, you often want to start with here's my conclusion, and then here's why, versus here's all the things I've done, here's all my thinking, here's all my data points, and then now here's my conclusion at the end of that. In business, people are like, "I'm bored. Just tell me what you think we should do and then help me understand why you got there."
turns.zh: 没错。这让我想起了“思维金字塔”模型。虽然我不打算深入探讨，但其核心理念是，在商业场合中，通常要先给出结论，再逐步展开论证。比如，先说“我的建议是……”，然后分点说明原因，最后总结观点。在商业场合，人们常说：“我没耐心了。直接告诉我该怎么做，然后帮我理解你的逻辑。”

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: The worst, which happens a lot is mixing all of those things with the action item or decision. So the action items and decisions are kind of interspersed randomly throughout a bunch of context, thought process, factors that you looked at, downside. It's like, it's all just interwoven, and so your reader doesn't know which parts are FYIs or which parts are background versus what is the thing that you want their response on, like what are you asking them to chime in on and what is the decision that we're actually trying to make? So if you do add all the thought process, I think splitting it up and making it clear that you're splitting it up, makes it so much more helpful for your reader.
turns.zh: 最糟糕的情况是把所有信息都混在一起，夹杂着行动项和决策内容。比如，行动项和决策被随意插入到大量背景信息、思考过程、考量因素和弊端分析之中。读者根本分不清哪些是背景信息，哪些是决策要点，更不明白你到底想让他们参与哪部分讨论，或者需要他们做出怎样的决策。所以，如果你确实要加入所有思考过程，我建议分段处理，并明确说明分隔内容，这对读者更有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And we'll link to all this stuff in the show notes, so don't feel like you have to remember all this. Okay, so this is a good time to get our fifth section and our fifth topic, which is around the skill of saying no. I feel like this is such an under-taught skill. I heard that Tim Ferriss was working on a book called The No Book, where he was going to share all the ways he's learned to say no, but I think he shelved it for whatever reason.
turns.zh: 太好了。我们会在节目笔记中附上所有相关内容，不用你全都记在心里。接下来是第五个部分和主题——学会说“不”。我觉得这是一项被严重忽视的技能。我听说蒂姆·费里斯曾在创作一本名为《说不》的书，分享自己学会说“不”的方法，但不知为何他搁置了这个项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I need advice on this, because I'm often asked for favors of all kinds and I am not amazing at saying no without being ... I try to be really nice about it and it takes time. And so I could use advice here. So I'm curious to hear your advice on saying no.
turns.zh: 我需要这方面的建议，因为经常有人请我帮忙，而我又不擅长拒绝别人。虽然我尽量委婉，但这太耗时间了。所以我很想听听大家的建议。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: Yeah. Saying no does not come naturally for me either as a recovering people pleaser. So I thought a lot about how to say no in ways that feel warm and respectful and respect the other person. So I think there's different ways to say no, depending on the situation and your relationship with that person.
turns.zh: 是啊，对我来说说“不”也很难，毕竟我曾是个讨好型人格。所以我一直在思考如何既保持温暖又尊重他人，同时又不让对方感到被冒犯。根据不同情境和与对方的关系，确实有不同的拒绝方式。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So within work, for example, saying no to your cross-functional team member or to your manager, that's very different than saying no to someone who doesn't know you on the internet, who is DMing you, asking you to help them with something.
turns.zh: 比如在工作中，拒绝跨部门同事或上司的请求，与在网上回复陌生人的DM请求，完全是两码事。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so with saying no with people that you have, let's say long term dynamics with, continuing dynamics, like a manager or a friend, et cetera, I usually like talking about the trade-offs of something. So this is something that I learned from Alex Peck, my coworker at altMBA, who's now CEO of altMBA. He was always great at this.
turns.zh: 面对那些与你有长期合作关系的人——比如上司、朋友等等，我通常喜欢谈论权衡利弊的问题。这是从我同事亚历克斯·佩克那里学到的。他现在是altMBA的首席执行官，他在这方面做得非常出色。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So when we worked together, he was my design counterpart and I would ask him like, "Hey, can you design this for me? Can you design that? And, oh, here's another thing I'm going to throw over the wall to you." And he was always so good at saying no in a way that felt good for me, the person who just asked him to do something. And I just thought that's pretty different, because usually when people say no, I'm a little irked or a little miffed.
turns.zh: 比如，当我们一起工作时，他是我的设计搭档。我会问他：“嘿，你能帮我设计这个吗？设计那个呢？哦，还有个新需求要交给你。” 他总是能用一种让我感觉良好的方式拒绝我，而这通常会让我有点不爽或生气。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So I thought, what is Alex doing that I can borrow from? And it turns out that Alex would always talk about trade-offs and he'd say, "Wes, yes, I can design this PDF for you. That means that the thing that I was going to work on today, which was redesigning this page on the site, will have to wait until later this week." Or, "This means that I'm going to be deprioritizing this other thing. Does that sound good to you? Or do you want me to prioritize the original design project you wanted me to work on?"
turns.zh: 于是我开始思考，亚历克斯做了什么值得我借鉴的地方？结果发现，他总会谈论权衡利弊。他会说：“韦斯，是的，我可以帮你设计这份PDF。但这意味着我今天原本要重新设计网站页面的工作就得推迟到本周晚些时候了。” 或者：“这意味着我要把其他事情的优先级降低。这样行吗？还是你希望我优先处理你最初要求的那个设计项目？”

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so for me hearing that it felt like I was in control and able to help him prioritize, basically. So it went from being a conversation about yes or no, are you a helpful person or are you not, are you a team player or are you not into, hey, how do we make sure that the important right things get done?
turns.zh: 对我来说，听到这些话感觉我能掌控局面，能帮助他合理分配时间。这样对话就不再是简单的“是”或“否”，而是关于你是否乐于助人，是否有团队精神，是否愿意一起想办法确保重要的事情得以完成。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: And so it's great for the person who you're saying no to and it's also great for Alex because whenever we had those conversations, I always thought that he was really thoughtful about making sure that the most important projects that we want to work on stayed prioritized.
turns.zh: 这种方式对被拒绝的人和亚历克斯本人都有好处。每次这样的对话后，我都觉得他考虑得非常周到，确保我们最想做的重要项目始终处于优先地位。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So it's a little bit of a work around. So you're not exactly saying no, but you're talking about trade-offs, which gets the result of the no. The reason why you want to say no is we don't have bandwidth to take everything on, but we feel weird about saying no to people because we're afraid that people are going to think we're not cooperative or whatever.
turns.zh: 这算是一种变通方法。你不必直接说“不”，但通过谈论权衡利弊就能达到拒绝的目的。拒绝别人的原因是我们没有精力承担所有任务，但又不想因为说“不”而显得不合作或有其他负面影响。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: So by talking about trade-offs, you really get the outcome, which is you protect your bandwidth, you protect your bandwidth, you protect your mental health, you protect your ability to do great work without feeling overly stretched, without actually even having to say the word no, which I just think is amazing.
turns.zh: 通过谈论权衡利弊，你能达成理想的结果——保护自己的精力、维护心理健康、确保工作质量不受影响，而无需直白地说“不”，我觉得这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a concept or a related concept that a manager once taught me, which is essentially the same idea, and she called it prioritize and communicate. And the idea here is someone gives you something to do that's not already in your plate, there's a two-by-two you can imagine in your head, there's, you can just prioritize it amongst your priorities and not communicate what you did and where it sits, or you could just communicate and not prioritize and that just means like, sorry, I don't have time for this right now. What you should do is prioritize it, here, it's going to sit in number three in my priority list, and communicate it, this is going to be third on my priority list, does this seem reasonable to you? Would you agree? Should I do this sooner or not? And that's a really good way of dealing with exactly what you're talking about. And so that's the little framework [inaudible 00:48:19]-
turns.zh: 这是经理曾教给我的一个概念或相关理念，核心思想是一致的，她称之为"优先排序与沟通"。具体来说，有人交给你一件超出你日常职责范围的任务。这时，你可以在脑中构想一个二维表格：要么在已有优先事项中为其排序，但不沟通进展；要么先沟通再排序，相当于说"抱歉，我现在没时间处理"。正确的做法应该是：将其列为第三优先事项，并明确告知对方，这样大家才能理解你的安排。这样做合理吗？你认同吗？我该早点处理还是再等等？这正是应对你所提问题的绝佳方法。

turns.speaker: Wes Kao
turns.en: I love that. I love a good two-by-two matrix and that is a fantastic one.
